meta.sourceDocument: Cambridge International AS & A Level Chemistry 9701 syllabus for 2025, 2026 and 2027 (version 1, September 2022)
meta.validFor: Exams in 2025, 2026 and 2027 (June and November series; March series in India)
meta.representation: Official subsection hierarchy plus normalized, source-checked numbered learning-outcome anchors for AS Topics 1–12. Remaining topics retain their scope-only boundary until extracted and cross-checked.

topics.title: Particles in the atom and atomic radius
outcomes: Understand that atoms are mostly empty space surrounding a very small, dense nucleus containing protons and neutrons, with electrons in shells around the nucleus.
Identify and describe protons, neutrons and electrons by their relative charges and masses.
Understand atomic number, proton number, mass number and nucleon number.
Describe the distribution of mass and charge within an atom.
Describe the behaviour of proton, neutron and electron beams moving at the same velocity in an electric field.
Determine the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in atoms and ions from atomic/proton number, mass/nucleon number and charge.
State and explain qualitatively the variations in atomic and ionic radii across a period and down a group.

topics.title: Isotopes
outcomes: Define an isotope in terms of its numbers of protons and neutrons.
Understand isotope notation using mass/nucleon number and atomic/proton number.
Explain why isotopes of the same element have the same chemical properties.
Explain why isotopes of the same element have different physical properties, limited to mass and density.

topics.title: Electrons, energy levels and atomic orbitals
outcomes: Understand shells, sub-shells, orbitals, principal quantum number n and ground state as applied to electronic configuration.
Describe the number of orbitals and maximum electrons in s, p and d sub-shells.
Describe the order of increasing sub-shell energy within the first three shells and the 4s and 4p sub-shells.
Describe electronic configurations by shell, sub-shell and orbital.
Explain electronic configurations in terms of electron energy and inter-electron repulsion.
Determine electronic configurations of atoms and ions from proton number and charge using full or shorthand notation.
Understand and use electrons-in-boxes notation.
Describe and sketch the shapes of s and p orbitals.
Describe a free radical as a species with one or more unpaired electrons.

topics.title: Ionisation energy
outcomes: Define and use first ionisation energy, IE.
Construct equations representing first, second and subsequent ionisation energies.
Identify and explain trends in ionisation energies across periods and down groups.
Identify and explain variation in successive ionisation energies of an element.
Understand ionisation energies as arising from attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron.
Explain ionisation-energy factors using nuclear charge, atomic/ionic radius, shielding and spin-pair repulsion.
Deduce electronic configurations from successive ionisation-energy data.
Deduce an element's position in the Periodic Table from successive ionisation-energy data.

sections.title: Atoms, molecules and stoichiometry
sections.summary: Atoms, molecules and stoichiometry. 4 official syllabus subsections.

topics.title: Relative masses of atoms and molecules
outcomes: Define the unified atomic mass unit as one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
Define relative atomic mass, relative isotopic mass, relative molecular mass and relative formula mass in terms of the unified atomic mass unit.

topics.title: The mole and the Avogadro constant
outcomes: Define and use the mole in terms of the Avogadro constant.

topics.title: Formulas
outcomes: Write ionic-compound formulas from ionic charges and oxidation numbers, including predicting ionic charge from Periodic Table position and recalling the specified common ions.
Write and construct balanced equations, including ionic equations without spectator ions, and use appropriate state symbols.
Define and use empirical and molecular formula.
Understand and use anhydrous, hydrated and water of crystallisation.
Calculate empirical and molecular formulas from given data.

topics.title: Reacting masses and volumes (of solutions and gases)
outcomes: Perform mole calculations involving reacting masses and percentage yield, gas volumes, solution volumes and concentrations, and limiting and excess reagents.
Deduce stoichiometric relationships from mole calculations.

topics.title: Electronegativity and bonding
outcomes: Define electronegativity as the power of an atom to attract electrons to itself.
Explain factors influencing electronegativity using nuclear charge, atomic radius and shielding by inner shells and sub-shells.
State and explain electronegativity trends across a period and down a group.
Use Pauling electronegativity differences to predict ionic or covalent bonding.

topics.title: Ionic bonding
outcomes: Define ionic bonding as electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
Describe ionic bonding using sodium chloride, magnesium oxide and calcium fluoride as examples.

topics.title: Metallic bonding
outcomes: Define metallic bonding as electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.

topics.title: Covalent bonding and coordinate (dative covalent) bonding
outcomes: Define covalent bonding as electrostatic attraction between two nuclei and a shared pair of electrons, and describe covalent bonding in the specified molecules and expanded-octet examples.
Describe coordinate (dative covalent) bonding, including formation of NH4+ from ammonia and hydrogen chloride and bonding in Al2Cl6.
Describe sigma and pi bonds using orbital overlap, apply them to H2, C2H6, C2H4, HCN and N2, use sp/sp2/sp3 hybridisation, and relate bond energy and bond length to covalent reactivity.

topics.title: Shapes of molecules
outcomes: State and explain molecular shapes and bond angles using VSEPR theory for the specified examples.
Predict shapes and bond angles in molecules and ions analogous to the specified VSEPR examples.

topics.title: Intermolecular forces, electronegativity and bond properties
outcomes: Describe hydrogen bonding in molecules containing N-H and O-H groups and use it to explain anomalous properties of water.
Use electronegativity to explain bond polarity and molecular dipole moments.
Describe van der Waals' forces, including instantaneous dipole-induced dipole and permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces, including hydrogen bonding.
State that ionic, covalent and metallic bonding are generally stronger than intermolecular forces.

topics.title: Dot-and-cross diagrams
outcomes: Use dot-and-cross diagrams to illustrate ionic, covalent and coordinate bonding, including species with expanded octets or odd numbers of electrons.

sections.title: States of matter
sections.summary: States of matter. 2 official syllabus subsections.

topics.title: The gaseous state: ideal and real gases and pV = nRT
outcomes: Explain the origin of gas pressure in terms of collisions between gas molecules and container walls.
Understand that an ideal gas has negligible particle volume and no intermolecular attractions.
Use pV = nRT in calculations, including determination of relative molecular mass.

topics.title: Bonding and structure
outcomes: Describe the lattice structures of giant ionic, simple molecular, giant molecular and giant metallic crystalline solids, using the specified examples.
Describe, interpret and predict how structure and bonding affect melting point, boiling point, electrical conductivity and solubility.
Deduce the structure and bonding of a substance from given information.

topics.title: Enthalpy change, ΔH
outcomes: Understand that chemical reactions involve enthalpy changes and can be exothermic or endothermic.
Construct and interpret reaction pathway diagrams showing reaction enthalpy change and activation energy.
Define and use standard conditions and the specified enthalpy-change terms: reaction, formation, combustion and neutralisation.
Understand energy transfer during reactions as arising from breaking and making chemical bonds.
Use bond energies to calculate enthalpy changes of reaction.
Understand that some bond energies are exact while others are average values.
Calculate enthalpy changes from experimental results using q = mcΔT and ΔH = -mcΔT/n.

topics.title: Hess’s law
outcomes: Apply Hess's law to construct simple energy cycles.
Use energy cycles and relevant energy terms to calculate enthalpy changes that cannot be measured directly and to use bond-energy data.

topics.title: Redox processes: electron transfer and changes in oxidation number (oxidation state)
outcomes: Calculate oxidation numbers of elements in compounds and ions.
Use changes in oxidation numbers to help balance chemical equations.
Explain and use redox, oxidation, reduction and disproportionation in terms of electron transfer and oxidation-number changes.
Explain and use oxidising agent and reducing agent.
Use Roman numerals to indicate oxidation-number magnitude.

topics.title: Electrolysis
outcomes: Describe electrolysis in terms of electron transfer and electrode reactions.
Predict products at electrodes using electrolyte state, ion position in the redox series and concentration.
Use half-equations and overall equations to describe electrolysis.

topics.title: Chemical equilibria: reversible reactions, dynamic equilibrium
outcomes: Understand reversible reactions, dynamic equilibrium as equal forward and reverse rates with constant concentrations, and the need for a closed system.
Define Le Chatelier's principle and use it to deduce qualitative equilibrium shifts caused by temperature, concentration, pressure or catalysts.
Deduce Kc expressions and carry out Kc calculations.
Use mole fraction and partial pressure and deduce Kp expressions.
Use Kc and Kp expressions for calculations without requiring quadratic equations.
Calculate equilibrium quantities from appropriate data.
State whether temperature, concentration, pressure or a catalyst changes the equilibrium constant.
Describe and explain Haber-process and Contact-process conditions as applications of dynamic equilibrium and Le Chatelier's principle.

topics.title: Brønsted–Lowry theory of acids and bases
outcomes: State the specified common acids and their formulas.
State the specified common alkalis and their formulas.
Describe the Brønsted-Lowry theory of acids and bases.
Describe strong acids/bases as fully dissociated and weak acids/bases as partially dissociated in aqueous solution.
Relate pH 7 to neutral water and distinguish acidic and alkaline solution pH ranges.
Explain qualitative differences between strong and weak acids, including reaction with a reactive metal and differences in pH measured by pH meter, universal indicator or conductivity.
Understand neutralisation as H+(aq) and OH-(aq) forming H2O(l).
Understand that salts are formed in neutralisation reactions.
Sketch pH titration curves for combinations of strong and weak acids with strong and weak alkalis.
Select suitable indicators for acid-alkali titrations from given data.

topics.title: Rate of reaction
outcomes: Explain and use rate of reaction, collision frequency, effective collisions and non-effective collisions.
Explain qualitatively how concentration and pressure affect reaction rate through the frequency of effective collisions.
Use experimental data to calculate reaction rate.

topics.title: Effect of temperature on reaction rates and the concept of activation energy
outcomes: Define activation energy, EA, as the minimum energy required for an effective collision.
Sketch and use the Boltzmann distribution to explain the significance of activation energy.
Explain qualitatively how temperature changes reaction rate using the Boltzmann distribution and frequency of effective collisions.

topics.title: Homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts
outcomes: Explain catalyst and catalysis, including that a catalyst provides a different mechanism with lower activation energy, the Boltzmann-distribution explanation, and reaction-pathway diagrams with and without an effective catalyst.

sections.title: The Periodic Table: chemical periodicity
sections.summary: The Periodic Table: chemical periodicity. 3 official syllabus subsections.

topics.title: Periodicity of physical properties of the elements in Period 3
outcomes: Describe qualitative periodic variations in atomic radius, ionic radius, melting point and electrical conductivity across Period 3.
Explain melting-point and electrical-conductivity variation in terms of structure and bonding.

topics.title: Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3
outcomes: Describe and write equations for Period 3 element reactions with oxygen, chlorine and water where specified.
State and explain oxidation-number variation in specified Period 3 oxides and chlorides using outer-shell electrons.
Describe and write equations for reactions of specified Period 3 oxides with water and identify likely solution pH.
Describe, explain and write equations for acid-base behaviour of specified Period 3 oxides and hydroxides, including relevant amphoteric behaviour.
Describe, explain and write equations for reactions of specified Period 3 chlorides with water and identify likely solution pH.
Explain trends in Period 3 chemical properties using bonding and electronegativity.
Suggest bonding types in specified chlorides and oxides from chemical and physical properties.

topics.title: Chemical periodicity of other elements
outcomes: Predict characteristic properties of an element in a given group using chemical periodicity.
Deduce the nature, possible Periodic Table position and identity of unknown elements from physical and chemical property data.

topics.title: Similarities and trends in the properties of the Group 2 metals, magnesium to barium, and their compounds
outcomes: Describe and write equations for Group 2 elements reacting with oxygen, water and dilute hydrochloric and sulfuric acids.
Describe and write equations for Group 2 oxides, hydroxides and carbonates reacting with water and dilute hydrochloric and sulfuric acids.
Describe and write equations for thermal decomposition of Group 2 nitrates and carbonates, including the trend in thermal stability.
Describe and predict trends in physical and chemical properties of the Group 2 elements and their compounds.
State the variation in solubilities of Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates.

topics.title: Physical properties of the Group 17 elements
outcomes: Describe the colours and volatility trend of chlorine, bromine and iodine.
Describe and explain the trend in bond strength of halogen molecules.
Interpret volatility in terms of instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces.

topics.title: The chemical properties of the halogen elements and the hydrogen halides
outcomes: Describe relative reactivity of halogen elements as oxidising agents.
Describe reactions of halogen elements with hydrogen and explain their relative reactivity.
Describe relative thermal stabilities of hydrogen halides and explain them using bond strengths.

topics.title: Some reactions of the halide ions
outcomes: Describe relative reactivity of halide ions as reducing agents.
Describe and explain halide-ion reactions with aqueous silver ions followed by aqueous ammonia and with concentrated sulfuric acid, including balanced equations.

topics.title: The reactions of chlorine
outcomes: Describe and interpret chlorine reactions with cold and hot aqueous sodium hydroxide in terms of oxidation-number changes and identify them as disproportionation.
Explain, including with an equation, the use of chlorine in water purification, including formation of HOCl and ClO- active species.

sections.title: Nitrogen and sulfur
sections.summary: Nitrogen and sulfur. 1 official syllabus subsection.

topics.title: Nitrogen and sulfur
outcomes: Explain nitrogen's low reactivity using triple-bond strength and lack of polarity.
Describe and explain ammonia basicity, ammonium-ion structure and formation, and displacement of ammonia from ammonium salts using acid-base reactions.
State and explain natural and man-made occurrences of nitrogen oxides and their catalytic removal from internal-combustion-engine exhaust.
Understand that NO and NO2 can react with unburned hydrocarbons to form PAN, a component of photochemical smog.
Describe the role of NO and NO2 in acid-rain formation, including catalytic oxidation of atmospheric sulfur dioxide.
